name: Obtain specialist consultations in the emergency department
summary: When an emergency physician needs a specialist to see, operate on or admit a patient, the unit clerk pages the on-call internist, hospitalist, surgeon, paediatrician or obstetrician, who calls back, takes a phone referral and then comes to the ED. Consultants are usually busy on the wards, in clinic or in the operating room and often come in from home at night, so the patient waits on an ED stretcher for hours. The consultant may order more tests before deciding to admit, operate or discharge with follow-up, and some referrals bounce to another service.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation with about 160,000 ED visits a year, on-call specialists with admitting privileges paid by OHIP, and no resident trainees.
baseline.notes: Specialists are not hospital employees; on-call duties are set by the professional staff rules. Mental health consultations run through a separate crisis assessment process.

trigger: An emergency physician decides that a specialist must see, operate on or admit the patient.
end_state: The specialist has given phone advice, admitted the patient (bed request sent), booked emergency surgery, or returned the patient to the emergency physician for discharge with a follow-up plan.

volume.seasonality: Rises with winter admissions (respiratory illness); surgical consults peak in summer and on weekends with injuries.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: about 15% of physician-seen ED visits (12,600 a month). OAG 2023 reports about 12% of Ontario ED visits were admitted in 2022/23, and almost all admissions here go through a consultation, plus consultations ending in discharge; a two-hospital Canadian tertiary study found at least one consultation for 38% of patients (cjem_consult_rates), higher than expected in a community hospital.

surge.cause: Winter respiratory virus season (influenza and RSV; COVID-19 waves from 2020)

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file's process map entry (author's estimate of the usual December-March rise in Ontario ED visits); no period source was opened that quantifies it.

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Electronic bed board and patient flow dashboard
Radiology information system, PACS and voice recognition dictation
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones

steps.name: Decide a consultation is needed
steps.description: The emergency physician, having seen the patient and the first results, decides that a specialist must see the patient or accept them for admission, picks the service and asks the unit clerk to page the on-call physician.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; in Ontario community hospitals admission goes through the accepting service, so most admissions start with a consultation.

steps.name: Find the on-call physician and page
steps.description: The unit clerk looks up the service's on-call schedule on the intranet or the switchboard list, pages or phones the physician and records the page time on the tracking board.

error.defect_description: Wrong service or out-of-date on-call schedule; the wrong physician is paged.

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of ED paging; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Consultant returns the page
steps.description: The on-call physician, often in clinic, on the ward or in the operating room, calls back when free. If there is no answer within about 15-30 minutes the clerk pages again or escalates to the backup.

control.basis: Hospital professional staff rules: on-call physicians must answer pages and attend the ED within set times (Public Hospitals Act medical staff by-laws)

next.condition: no answer or wrong physician: page again

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014 name urgent ward issues and simultaneous ED consultations as major contributors to consultation delay; callback times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Give the referral by phone
steps.description: The emergency physician presents the patient by phone: complaint, findings, results, what has been done and the question for the specialist, such as admission, surgery or follow-up advice.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Consultant decides how to respond
steps.description: The specialist decides whether to give advice by phone, come and see the patient now, or come after finishing the current list, and whether they need to travel in from home after hours.

next.condition: medicine or other specialty: comes in from home after hours
medicine or other specialty: in hospital
surgery: comes in from home after hours

evidence.note: Service mix is the author's estimate for a community hospital where internal medicine and hospitalists take most admissions.

steps.name: Document telephone advice
steps.description: The emergency physician records the specialist's advice, changes treatment or arranges clinic follow-up as advised, and keeps responsibility for the patient.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Travel in from home
steps.description: After hours the on-call specialist drives in from home, usually 15 to 40 minutes, after finishing any phone orders for the ward.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of suburban travel times.

steps.name: Medicine or specialty consultant assesses the patient
steps.description: The internist, hospitalist or other specialist reviews the ED record and results, takes their own history and examines the patient, often after finishing ward rounds or clinic patients first.

control.basis: Hospital professional staff rules: on-call physicians must answer pages and attend the ED within set times (Public Hospitals Act medical staff by-laws)

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014: median 55 minutes (IQR 21-115) from request to consultant arrival and 58 minutes (IQR 25-126) from arrival to decision at three Canadian tertiary centres; community on-call waits and branch shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Surgeon assesses the patient
steps.description: The general surgeon or orthopaedic surgeon on call sees the patient between operating room cases or after the list ends, examines them and reviews imaging.

control.basis: Hospital professional staff rules: on-call physicians must answer pages and attend the ED within set times (Public Hospitals Act medical staff by-laws)

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014 timings; surgeons finishing elective lists before attending is the author's general knowledge; shares estimated.

steps.name: Paediatrician assesses the child
steps.description: The paediatrician on call sees the child in the ED, often coming from the paediatric ward or the nursery, and decides on admission or discharge with follow-up.

control.basis: Hospital professional staff rules: on-call physicians must answer pages and attend the ED within set times (Public Hospitals Act medical staff by-laws)

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014 timings; paediatric shares estimated.

steps.name: Obstetrician-gynaecologist assesses the patient
steps.description: The obstetrician on call, usually in the birthing unit, sees early-pregnancy bleeding, ectopic pregnancy or gynaecological pain in the ED.

control.basis: Hospital professional staff rules: on-call physicians must answer pages and attend the ED within set times (Public Hospitals Act medical staff by-laws)

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014 timings; obstetric shares estimated.

steps.name: Surgeon travels in from home
steps.description: After hours the surgeon on call drives in from home, usually 15 to 40 minutes, to see a patient who may need an operation, sometimes after arranging the operating room team by phone.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for tests the consultant ordered
steps.description: The consultant orders further blood work, ultrasound or CT and the patient waits on the stretcher for the results before the specialist decides. No one works on the consultation while it waits.

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014 list the need for additional laboratory or imaging tests as a major contributor to consultation delay; duration is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Consultant reviews results and decides
steps.description: The specialist reviews the new results, re-examines if needed and decides on admission, surgery or discharge with follow-up, or hands the patient to a more suitable service.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; consultant_specialist stands in for whichever specialist ordered the tests.

steps.name: Write admission orders and consult note
steps.description: The admitting physician writes the consultation note and admission orders in the hospital system, choosing the unit and level of care, and the patient becomes their responsibility.

control.basis: Admission only by a physician with admitting privileges (Public Hospitals Act and medical staff by-laws)

evidence.note: Author's estimate; consultant_specialist stands in for surgeons, paediatricians and obstetricians who admit.

steps.name: Book emergency surgery and admit
steps.description: The surgeon books the case with the operating room charge nurse by priority category, gets consent, writes pre-operative and admission orders and tells anaesthesia.

control.basis: Informed consent to treatment (Ontario Health Care Consent Act)

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of emergency OR booking; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Write recommendations for discharge
steps.description: The specialist writes a consult note with treatment recommendations and arranges a clinic appointment or fracture clinic follow-up, then hands the patient back to the emergency physician.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Send the bed request
steps.description: The unit clerk enters the bed request from the admission orders into the bed board, tells the charge nurse and the bed flow coordinator, and changes the most responsible physician on the tracking board.

error.defect_description: Bed request entered with the wrong service or isolation status.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Discharge with the consultant's plan
steps.description: The emergency physician reads the consultant's note, writes the discharge plan and prescriptions and confirms the follow-up appointment with the patient.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Hand over care to the admitting physician
steps.description: The emergency physician and the admitting physician agree the time responsibility changes, and the emergency nurse tells the patient and family the admission plan.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Page not answered
exceptions.description: The on-call physician does not call back in time and is paged again or the backup is called.

exceptions.name: Consultant orders more tests
exceptions.description: The specialist wants more blood work or imaging before deciding, adding hours on the stretcher.

exceptions.name: Referral bounced to another service
exceptions.description: The specialist decides the patient belongs to another service, and the paging starts again.

exceptions.name: Consultant comes in from home
exceptions.description: After hours the specialist travels in before seeing the patient.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from consultation request to the consultant's disposition decision (about 3 and 8 hours)

evidence.note: Author's estimate anchored on Lee et al. 2014 (median 138 minutes, IQR 82-239, at tertiary centres with residents in house) and lengthened for community on-call consultants who cover wards, clinics and the operating room and travel in after hours.

benchmarks.unit: minutes from consultation request to disposition decision
benchmarks.population: 285 ED patients at three Canadian tertiary care centres

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014.

benchmarks.unit: minutes from consultation request to consultant arrival
benchmarks.population: 285 ED patients at three Canadian tertiary care centres

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014.

benchmarks.population: 1,930 ED patients at two Canadian tertiary care EDs

evidence.note: CJEM study of consultation rates and complexity: 54.3% of consulted patients admitted; 38% of patients had at least one consultation.

pain_points.description: Consultants finish ward rounds, clinics or operating lists before coming to the ED, so the patient waits on a stretcher for hours.

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014: urgent ward issues and simultaneous ED consultations were major contributors to consultation delay.

pain_points.description: Consultants often order further tests before deciding, adding a second wait for results.

evidence.note: Lee et al. 2014: need for additional laboratory or radiographic investigations contributed to delay.

pain_points.description: Paging depends on accurate on-call lists and callbacks; unanswered pages and referrals bounced between services restart the clock.

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of ED consultation processes.

sources.title: Assessment of consultation impact on emergency department operations through novel metrics of responsiveness and decision-making efficiency
sources.publisher: Canadian Journal of Emergency Medicine, Cambridge University Press
sources.supports: Median 55 min request to consultant arrival, 58 min arrival to decision, 138 min total consultation time, ED length of stay 778 min, 285 patients at three Canadian tertiary centres; delay causes: urgent ward issues, simultaneous ED consultations, additional tests.

sources.title: Consultation outcomes in the emergency department: exploring rates and complexity
sources.publisher: Canadian Journal of Emergency Medicine, Cambridge University Press
sources.supports: At least one consultation for 38% of 1,930 patients at two tertiary EDs; 54.3% of consulted patients admitted; 92% had one consultation.

assumptions: The simulated median (about 3.8 hours) is about 1.3 times the estimated 3-hour benchmark and about 1.7 times the tertiary-centre median of 138 minutes (lee2014); the gap reflects community on-call consultants without residents, which is an estimate rather than a measured figure.

Hospitalists who admit most medical patients in Ontario community hospitals are folded into consultant_specialist because the organisation file does not list hospitalist among this process's roles; the hospitalist role exists in the organisation file.

Steps s14 and s15 use consultant_specialist for whichever specialist is deciding or admitting; surgeons, paediatricians and obstetricians do this work for their own patients, so their labour cost is slightly understated.
The consultation ends at the disposition decision with orders written; boarding until an inpatient bed is free is the admission-boarding workflow.
Mental health crisis consultations are in a separate process (mh-ed-crisis-assessment) and are excluded here.
The cycle-time benchmark is an estimate; the only Canadian timing study opened was at tertiary centres with residents, where consultants respond faster than community on-call physicians.
Stated FTE is the consultant time spent on ED consultations, an estimate cross-checked against hands-on time x volume.
